subject: ss-medical-oncology
title: Opioid receptors, ceiling effect, fentanyl patch and rescue dosing

steps.tx: Opioid-induced **respiratory depression** is driven mainly by the **mu opioid receptor**, which these drugs activate in the brainstem. Brainstem neurons become less responsive to rising **carbon dioxide** levels, so each breath is shallower and breathing slows. Sedation usually appears first, which makes it a useful early warning.
steps.say: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is driven mainly by the mu opioid receptor. These drugs act on brainstem neurons and make them less responsive to rising carbon dioxide levels, so each breath becomes shallower and breathing slows. Sedation usually comes first. A respiratory rate below 10 breaths per minute is an early warning sign that needs prompt attention.

nodes.label: Brainstem less responsive to carbon dioxide

steps.tx: **Naloxone** is a **pure antagonist** at the mu receptor that reverses opioid effects, including breathing depression. In an unstable patient it is given intravenously in **titrated** steps, starting with 0.4 milligrams (mg) diluted in 10 milliliters (mL) of saline. Each further 1 to 2 mL is given every 30 to 60 seconds until breathing improves.
steps.say: Naloxone is a pure antagonist, which means it blocks the mu receptor and reverses opioid effects, including breathing problems. In an unstable patient, clinicians give it intravenously in titrated steps. The first dose is 0.4 milligrams diluted in 10 milliliters of saline. Further doses of 1 to 2 milliliters follow every 30 to 60 seconds until breathing improves.

steps.tx: **Full agonists** such as morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone and methadone show **no ceiling effect** on pain relief. A higher dose can keep adding analgesia, so the correct dose is the one that controls the pain. By contrast, the **partial agonist** buprenorphine has a **ceiling effect**: beyond a certain dose, more drug gives no further analgesia.
steps.say: Full agonists, including morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone and methadone, have no ceiling effect on pain relief. A higher dose can keep adding analgesia, so the right dose is the one that controls the pain. Buprenorphine behaves differently. As a partial agonist, it reaches a plateau, and beyond a certain dose extra drug adds nothing to pain relief.

points: No ceiling effect on pain relief

right.title: Partial agonist (buprenorphine)
points: Lower potential for abuse than full agonists

steps.tx: A **transdermal fentanyl patch** stays on for **72 hours** and delivers steady drug levels. Pain relief starts late, because of an **onset delay** of about 12 to 15 hours after placement. Levels then need a further 24 to 72 hours to equilibrate, so a **short-acting rescue** opioid is needed at the start, and dose changes should wait at least 72 hours.
steps.say: A transdermal fentanyl patch stays on for 72 hours and gives steady drug levels. Pain relief starts late, with a delay of about 12 to 15 hours after placement. Levels then take another 24 to 72 hours to settle, so a short-acting rescue opioid is essential at the beginning. Dose changes should wait at least 72 hours.

steps.tx: Fentanyl suits patients who cannot take oral medicines, and it is linked to **less constipation** than oral morphine in some studies. Because the liver clears it without active metabolites, it is a reasonable option in **renal insufficiency** (reduced kidney function). However, **cachexia** (severe wasting) removes much of the **subcutaneous fat** (fat under the skin) that absorbs the patch, so levels may fall short.
steps.say: Fentanyl suits patients who cannot take oral medicines. Some studies show it causes less constipation than oral morphine. Because the liver clears it without producing active metabolites, it is a reasonable choice when kidney function is reduced. Patients with cachexia, however, carry little fat under the skin, and absorption from the patch can fall short.

left.title: Advantages
points: Less constipation than oral morphine in some studies
No active metabolites from liver breakdown
Useful when oral intake is not possible

right.title: Cautions
points: Little subcutaneous fat, as in cachexia, lowers absorption
Heat over the patch increases absorption
Patches with metal need removal before magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Dose changes no sooner than every 72 hours

steps.tx: **Breakthrough pain** is severe acute pain on top of chronic pain that is otherwise controlled, and it needs a short-acting **rescue dose**. For a patient on a fixed schedule, the rescue dose is typically **5 to 15 percent** of the total 24-hour opioid requirement. Liquid morphine rescue is sometimes sized at about 20 percent of the baseline dose instead.
steps.say: Breakthrough pain is severe pain that breaks through an otherwise controlled regimen, and it needs a short-acting rescue dose. For a patient on a fixed schedule, the rescue dose is usually 5 to 15 percent of the total 24 hour requirement. Take a patient on 300 milligrams of oral morphine a day: the rescue dose would be roughly 15 to 45 milligrams. Liquid morphine is sometimes sized at 20 percent instead.

steps.tx: A **fentanyl patch** is meant only for **opioid-tolerant** patients with chronic pain. Because the patch takes many hours to act, a short-acting opioid should cover the early gap, and the result should not be judged until the equilibration period has passed. **Heat over the patch**, from a fever or a heating pad, can speed absorption and lead to respiratory depression.
steps.say: A fentanyl patch is meant only for patients who are already opioid tolerant and have chronic pain. Because it takes many hours to act, a short-acting opioid should cover the early gap. Wait for the equilibration period before judging the result. Heat over the patch, from a fever or a heating pad, can speed absorption and lead to breathing problems.
